speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
That this House recognizes the unnecessary hardship inflicted on older Canadian workers by the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which cause pension benefits to be considered earned income for unemployment insurance purposes, and since votes on opposition motions are no longer considered a question of confidence in the Government, therefore urges the Government to repeal those changes immediately.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have considered this to be an extremely important motion and I have waited until the appropriate moment to enter such a motion, waited because this House changed the rules. We are going to have an opportunity to vote under a new rule which says that these kinds of votes are not considered confidence in the Government. Members on all sides of the House, and I appeal particularly to the Government side, are perfectly free to vote their conscience on this question without any fear of bringing down the Government. The vote will not result in an election. I appeal to Government Members to listen to the debate and to be persuaded by the pointed arguments that we are going to present here today.
More important, Mr. Speaker, I know that within the Government caucus there has been a considerable amount of unrest about this whole question of the changes regarding pension income and unemployment insurance. 1 know as well from reading the press that Members on all sides of the House are being petitioned by their constituents to remove this inequitable change to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
When did this change come into effect? When was it announced? I think it is important to go back and trace its history. This change was announced on November 8, 1984 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), along with another change regarding severance pay and holiday pay, and it was done without any consultation. There was no consulting with Opposition Members; there was no consulting the people of Canada and there was no consulting the trade union movement. It was a unilateral decision taken by the Minister of Finance and it was supposed to come into effect on December 31, 1984.
Because of a considerable amount of pressure, not only from Members on this side of the House but from within the Conservative caucus, and a considerable amount of representation from Canadians, from the Armed Forces, for example, the Government announced that the pension change would take effect on January 1, 1986.
The Government said in its November 8 statement that it hoped to save about $30 million with this change. That was the purpose for the change, that the Government would save $30
March 20, 1986

million in the Unemployment Insurance Program. There was no consultation, Mr. Speaker.
In the spring of 1985 the Government decided it ought to take a look at the unemployment insurance program. The Forget Commission was set up. Mr. Claude Forget was made the chairman of a commission to study the unemployment insurance program. The Commission was supposed to report in the spring of 1986, but it will not do that until the fall of 1986 because of the considerable amount of response it has received.
The Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council tabled its annual report in August, 1985. There amidst its recommendations is this one:
That the Government not proceed with the announced changes in the Unemployment Insurance Regulations scheduled to take place January 1, 1986, regarding the identification of pension as income for the period immediately following lay-off, until the Commission of Inquiry on Unemployment Insurance has reviewed the issue and made recommendations.
The Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council has advised the Government it ought not to go ahead with the change until the Forget Commission has reported.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, I personally have entered in this House petitions from across the country containing over 19,000 signatures. Other Members of this House have also entered petitions calling upon the Government not to proceed with this provision. One of the members of the Forget Commission itself, Mr. Roy Bennett, a former executive with Ford Motor Company, has spoken out. On February 14, 1986 The Winnipeg Free Press reported:
"In hindsight, I think it would have been better had the Government not made those changes", Roy Bennett a former president of Ford Motors said in an interview.
"While we understand the motivation behind them, the're not well founded. To the extent the changes were made, they should have been different from the ones that were implemented."
From the Forget Commission itself in February we have members of the Commission saying that the changes ought not to have been made, and if they were made they ought not to have been made in the form that they were.
From the government benches we have the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) who raised a question in the House asking the Government to withdraw the changes until the Forget Commission had reported. I quote from the article:
Outside the Commons, Nowlan told reporters that most Conservative MPs had complained about the new rules and said he was disappointed by MacDonald's answer.
"I just can't understand her opinion," Nowlan said. "Flora's either blinded because she's so busy with work or she has been completely captivated by her officials on this issue. It's not the Flora MacDonald who used to show compassion and concern for the underdog."
Hear, hear, Mr. Speaker. The Member was absolutely correct about that. We have letters from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen). The Defence Minister wrote to the Minister of Employment and Immigration on June 26, 1985. In the letter he said:
Supply
After considering the options available, I have now concluded that the only reasonable and fair approach is to seek an exemption for the Canadian Forces from those provisions beginning 1 January, 1986 that will require pension income to be treated as earnings for purposes of determining Unemployment Insurance Benefits.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote this to the Minister of Employment:
As you are aware, because of the unique requirements of military service, members of the Canadian Forces are required to retire at a much earlier age than people in other walks of life. Generally, military personnel qualify for an annuity after reaching twenty years of service. They may retire voluntarily at this point, or continue serving until compulsory retirement, which may occur as early as age forty or as late as age fifty-five.
Still young individuals, Mr. Speaker.
In addition to that, we have had hundreds of letters from across the country written to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) with copies sent to myself and other Members of this House in which people call upon the Minister to withdraw the particular provision.
I have one from a gentleman in Winnipeg, Mr. Elmar A. Duell. He wrote:
I have attentively listened to the Budget, in the vain hope to hear the announcement which would rescind your barbaric changes, as implemented on January 5 with respect to the "pensions" being accounted as earned income for UIC purposes.
The P.C. Women's Association in Oromocto-Burton-Geary passed a resolution calling upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to withdraw the inequitable provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act. They gave the resolution to their Member of Parliament, the Hon. Member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Howie) who was supposed to have delivered it to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. After all of the clear indication from the opposition and government sides of the House, from people across the country, including Conservative associations, and from Ministers of the Crown, the Government's response has been a consistent "no", that the changes would proceed. Indeed, the changes have been implemented.
The Minister's rationale is that notice was given over a year ago. What difference does it make whether notice was given over a year ago? The effects are still there and people are living with their effects. We know that the regulation was not drawn up until December of 1985. On December 13, 1985, the Minister wrote to me in response to suggestions 1 had made about the regulations. She said:
At this stage, I can only inform you that no final decisions have been made by the Government concerning the specific applications of the regulations. However, 1 wish to thank you for your suggestion on this matter.
The date of that letter is December 13, 1985, and the change came into effect on January 5, 1986. At that point the regulation had not been drawn up and the Minister could easily have gotten off the galloping horse by simply withdrawing the regulation.
Canadians, including members of the New Democratic Party, are opposed to the change because it is unfair in its application. Not all pensions are treated in the same way. Only

March 20, 1986
Supply
pensions earned as a result of work are affected. Pensions from RRSPs or annuities are not counted. Pensions from the American, British, or French army are not counted. Only pensions from the Canadian Armed Forces are counted, so the rule is unfair in its application.
Another point of unfairness is that people who are disentitled from receiving UI benefits still have to pay the premiums. If a person has taken early retirement and then gets another job, he will have to pay premiums but will never be able to collect unemployment insurance. In what sort of insurance program does one pay premiums but has no hope of collecting at all? A person who has taken an early retirement, is receiving a pension, takes another job, and then becomes sick, cannot get any sick benefits at all through the unemployment insurance program. That is highly unfair.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, there are all sorts of opportunities to run around the ends of the change. For example, if you work for a large enough organization which is prepared to play ball with you, you can postpone receiving your pension for a year while you collect unemployment insurance benefits for 49 weeks. Of course, in the following year you can get an increase in your pension to make up for the year you postponed it. That does not seem fair to me at all. What we are really doing is means testing the unemployment insurance program because it is the pension which you receive which determines whether or not you get unemployment insurance.
Another reason we opposed this change is that it is contradictory. In the Sudbury Basin the price of minerals has not been very good. The major employees in a single-industry community, Inco and Falconbridge, told the workers that they wanted to protect the jobs of younger workers by offering an early retirement prorgram. The employees were told that if they took the early retirement program they would be eligible for unemployment insurance providing they were looking for, and available to work. By taking early retirement they would protect the jobs of younger workers.
Many older workers felt that was their opportunity to do something else which they had always wanted to do, so they took early retirement in the hopes of protecting the jobs of younger workers. We were pretty happy in our community that approximately 1,200 older workers took early retirement, because it protected the jobs of younger workers who were starting out in life and had all the high expenses of maintaining a young family. After these workers accepted early retirement there was an arbitrary and unilateral move to make them ineligible for unemployment insurance. Why does the Government on the one hand encourage older workers to consider early retirement to protect the jobs of younger workers, while on the other hand pulling the rug out from under them? That is extremely contradictory.
We also oppose this, Mr. Speaker, because we believe it to be illegal. The Supreme Court of Canada decided the Dalliali-an case with respect to a person who had been collecting unemployment insurance at age 64 and then turned 65. The Act said that when one reaches the age of 65 one does not pay premiums, but cannot collect benefits. The person had started
the claim before turning 65, and the moment he turned 65 the Unemployment Insurance Commission cut him off. The Supreme Court of Canada ruled that a law cannot be made which retroactively takes benefits away from individuals.
Yet, in this particular case, all persons who were getting a pension and collecting unemployment insurance were cut off on January 5, 1986. I would extend the argument to say that anyone who was contributing to the unemployment insurance program at the time of the January 5 change ought to qualify for full benefits under the program. We argue against this because we believe it to be illegal.
We believe that the Government should immediately withdraw this provision. We believe that the purpose of the Forget Commission was to study the unemployment insurance program in totality and to make recommendations to Parliament with respect to how the program should apply. Changes are being made to the Act. The Minister says that this has been referred to the Forget Commission. In the meantime, thousands and thousands of claimants in the country are being denied unemployment insurance.
The Minister says that the Government can take a position when the Forget Commission reports in the fall. It could be months after the Forget Commission reports before Parliament passes a law. What will we then do about the people who did not get their benefits? They may not qualify. According to the Act you must have 20 insurable weeks in the preceding 52 weeks. By the time Parliament passes a law they may not qualify at all and will have been denied their benefits. It is extremely unfair to put people in that position.
At the National Economic Conference held here at the government Conference Centre before the Budget was introduced in May, 1985, 75 per cent of the participants, which represented predominantly the business sector and the trade union movement, signed a petition saying that the Government ought not to go ahead with these particular provisions. By not responding to what people are saying through their letters and petitions, the Government is harming people who have embarked in good faith on their unemployment insurance application and have been receiving benefits.
The only fair thing for the Government to do at this time is to withdraw this provision. I appeal to the conscience of Members on the Government side. You can vote freely knowing that it will not bring your Government down and cause an election. Under the new rules you can actually stand up and vote the way you have always said we in this House should vote, on the principal of an issue. Recognize the unfairness, the contradictory nature, and the possible illegality of this regulation. Let us put aside our partisan politics for the sake of the people who have in all honesty and good faith taken early retirement, or were forced to take early retirement as in the case of the Armed Forces. I say to Members on the Government side, put aside the partisanship for just 20 minutes this afternoon and vote for people who have been so brutally
March 20, 1986

treated by this change which came into effect on January 1, 1986.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext: Questions or comments.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 was interested in the comments of the Hon. Member relating to suddenly, at this stage, going back to where we were prior to January 1 and yanking the matter out of the purview, if you will, of the Forget Commission. As the Hon. Member indicated, there have been many comments from all sides, his party, the Official Opposition, and certainly by Government Members, who are most concerned about this issue and most sympathetic with the plight of the pensioners concerned. Suggestions on how to deal with the problem have come from the Government benches. I wonder what is the best way of dealing with the problem now that the regulations have been put in place and the matter referred to the Forget Commission in order to find an over-all solution, not only to this issue but all issues relating to unemployment insurance benefits.
I am sure the Hon. Member is supportive of the concept of the Forget Commission. I am sure he and his party are supportive of the approach of taking an over-all review of the problems concerning unemployment insurance. Three are many problems. Something has to be done to come up with a comprehensive position on this issue. The Hon. Member is a Member of a party which has long advocated global planning. The NDP is renowned for having advocated a planned economy in which all of the pieces are not examined individually or piecemeal but in a global context. The NDP has always advocated that unemployment not be looked at on its own but in the light of interests rates, exchange rates, monetary policy, the deficit and tax policy. The same is true of the NDP's point of view on the question of public ownership of various parts of the economy, whether it be the banks or the energy industry.
1 would like to know if the Hon. Member feels that we should be looking at this in a global sense. Should the Forget Commission make some global recommendations to straighten out the problems? It might have been nice to have this beforehand, but since we do not, is it not now more logical to leave it to the Forget Commission to come up with some global recommendations, the kind the NDP usually likes, rather than piecemeal recommendations?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
I think the Hon. Member is absolutely right. He has described the NDP's overview exactly correctly. I wrote to the Minister to tell her that she had not drawn up the regulations until late December, 1985, the change came into effect in 1986, yet the Forget Commission was set up in the spring of 1985. So we said that she should stop making changes before we look at the over-all issue. You cannot go chopping away piecemeal, taking $30 million here and $100 million there. Let the Forget Commission look at the whole program and make recommendations. Then we can make changes with some intelligence and some understanding of how these things hang together. When you start chopping away piecemeal you drastically affect people's lives. You have not
Supply
really prepared the ground for acceptance of the changes you want. That is why I appeal to the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) to support us and vote with us on this motion today.
The Hon. Member raised another very important question. It is not improper for us to now tell the Minister to withdraw the regulation. It is affecting people, denying them unemployment insurance. It is an unjust change. Let us withdraw it, wait until the Forget Commission brings down its recommendations, and maybe it will have a better approach. If so we would not be adverse to a better approach to unemployment insurance. We would support it. We would have no objection.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the most unusual feature of this particular change concerns a person who may have retired early from the Armed Forces, for example. He or she is in receipt of an Armed Forces pension and they now hold down a job. They would be ineligible under these changes to receive sick benefits under UIC during the time they continue to be employed. Would the Hon. member care to comment on the injustice of denying a person who is sick the benefit that they otherwise would be entitled to under the Unemployment Insurance Act?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. I did touch on that briefly. It was one of the unfair aspects of that particular provision. That is one of the reasons we oppose it. If a person retires early and goes out and gets another job, pays his premiums to the UIC and then gets laid off or becomes sick, he would not be able to collect the sick benefits he would be entitled to. He has paid the premiums, it is an insurance program, yet he would never be able to collect. We think that is the ultimate in unfairness. That is why we presented this motion today in the hope that Members on the Government side will see it the same way we see it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
I was intrigued by the Hon. Member's overview of what the insurance scheme actually is. We all remember when it was first implemented and 97 per cent of the gainfully employed contributed, that it was intended as a calamity insurance for those people who found themselves in the unfortunate situation of having no income. In retrospect the Hon. Member would agree there must have been instances in the past where individuals reaching toward early retirement, 62, 63, would find the opportunity to be able to take a sizeable package of money and then still draw on a plan to which the entire community is contributing but which should be used only for that calamity.
The insurance scheme, in my mind, was not intended as a guaranteed value life insurance, or a mutual fund. It is a form of term insurance to which we are all committing ourselves. 1 would ask him to reflect on some of the difficulties seen by those of us who are very concerned about bringing social assistance to those who really need it. I would certainly be the first one to join him in that kind of an opinion.

March 20, 1986

The Hon. Member referred to Mr. Roy Bennett and what he may or may not have said. I would just like to assure Mr. Speaker that Mr. Bennett has been in touch with the Deputy Minister and the Minister, and what Mr. Bennett says is that he would not make any specific recommendations or suggestions until the complete report of the commission of inquiry is submitted. Without trying to get into a debate on what may or may not have taken place, we know that Mr. Bennett, as a member of that commission, will be supporting and waiting for the final report to be submitted.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last point raised by the Parliamentary Secretary, I simply read his quote from a Canadian Press article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on February 14, 1986. I have been the UI critic for my Party from the time 1 was elected in 1972, so I am fairly well acquainted with the thrust and the over-all philosophy of the program. That is exactly why we said that they ought not to have made this change. It is out of place and it is out of context, and that is why it should have been looked at by the Forget Commission in totality. We do not insure individuals in the program, we insure their income. That is what we insure in the unemployment insurance program.
In the pre-1971 act, I may remind the Hon. Member, we used to pay one full year of unemployment insurance benefits on retirement. A person would collect a whole year of unemployment insurance benefits when he retired from his work. 1 say that to inform the hon. gentleman of one of the principles that used to be in the pre-1971 act.
What we were really dcing here was insuring the income of the individual, and in fact we protected the jobs of younger workers when older workers took an early retirement program. It is the choice of having them stay on the job and the younger worker going on unemployment insurance, or we encourage the older worker to take the early retirement and be eligible for unemployment benefits, which means he has to look for work, be capable and available for work.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 82-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT EFFECT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
I regret the Hon. Member's time has expired. Debate?
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to start by congratulating my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) for putting down this motion dealing with the cut-backs in unemployment insurance for those on early retirement pensions. We have had an opportunity to raise this matter in the House before by way of questions to Ministers, by statements pursuant to Standing Order 21 and by petitions, but this is the first time we have had a chance to debate the issue at any great length and to vote on the issue.
It is rather shocking to consider that this important change in unemployment insurance was implemented without any debate initiated by the Government and without any vote. This is a very important change in unemployment insurance affecting thousands of Canadians without any debate sponsored by the Government or any chance for the House to vote on it.
What is also important about this resolution today is that it is the first time that we will be voting on an Opposition motion which does not express non-confidence in the Government. That is extremely significant because it gives all Members in the House, in the Opposition and on the Government benches, an opportunity to really represent their constituents. Their constituents will be watching them and will know the vote this evening will be one that cannot topple the Government, that does not express non-confidence in the Government. As a matter of fact the House urges the Government to withdraw the policy. That is what we will be voting on. We will be testing the sincerity of the Government with respect to these new rules. When the Government implemented the new rules it said this would bring in a new dawning, a new spirit in the House of Commons whereby Members will be able to express their views more readily and with greater freedom.
These changes in the unemployment insurance are cruel, insensitive, retroactive, inequitable and unfair. Unfortunately, I do not think the Parliamentary Secretary, who just asked a question, has read the Act closely. He just said that unemployment insurance was meant to help those people with no income. That is not what unemployment insurance is, and there is nowhere in the Act that it says that. Unemployment insurance is insurance for those who are unemployed. For example, if a person is retired early and collects rent, collects dividends, collects interest, has a partnership in a business and collects profits, they do not cut back their unemployment insurance. You could have somebody unemployed who does not have an early retirement pension but he owns a series of flats and he collects rent and he collects his unemployment insurance. But the poor fellow in the Armed Forces who is getting a pension, he has his unemployment cut back. So it is not, as the Parliamentary Secretary said, insurance against loss of income, but rather insurance against loss of employment. I would like to get that straight.
He also asked why people 62 and 63 should get unemployment insurance when they are getting a pension? I must point out to him that there are people being affected by this measure who are in their forties and fifties. In the Armed Forces you can be retired at 45 and have to go on pension. I have a file full of letters from people in their fifties on early retirement who were collecting unemployment insurance and were cut back. Many still have children in university. Many people were going to use these early retirement pensions to roll them over, at least part of them, into RSPs for the day when they really retired, because they had to go back to work or they hopefully were going to go get another job.
This change is retroactive, it is cruel, it is insensitive and it is inequitable. There are many people who have paid into the unemployment insurance system for 30, 35 years and never collected. Suddenly they are forced out on an early retirement and they are finding when they went to collect now they cannot do so. That is not fair. Unemployment insurance is not a welfare program and was never meant to be a welfare program. It is an insurance program, and I just made some arguments in that respect. We never cut back unemployment
March 20, 1986

insurance for people collecting rent, interest, dividends or profits, and the Government has not done that yet. If they were being consistent they would do that, but I think the policy is wrong in the first place.
I also want to point out that a good percentage of these people who are being cut back are on early retirement pensions but are still looking for work. They have to look for work because some of them have children. These are people my age and the age of the Parliamentary Secretary. They have children going to school, and have family responsibilities.
Every time we put a question to the Minister about this policy her justification for it is that it was announced a year in advance. Even advance notice of one year does not make a bad policy good, or justify the program. That argument is unacceptable. Furthermore, these changes are illogical. The Government makes significant changes to unemployment insurance then sets up the Forget Commission to study the unemployment insurance system with a view to making recommendations for change. However, this is done after the Government has already made very significant changes. How, in the name of reason, can that be justified? What is the purpose of establishing the Forget Commission to study the system when the Government has already made unfair cut-backs in unemployment insurance to thousands of Canadians?
I would like the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary to respond to that. Incidentally, I suggest it is an indication of the importance the Government places on this matter when the Minister who is responsible is not even here to respond in this debate. The Parliamentary Secretary is here-

speechtext:
I regret to inform the Hon. Member that his time has expired. Resuming debate with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Weiner).
Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Employment and Immigration): Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to have this opportunity to speak on unemployment insurance. It is, indeed, a pleasure to represent the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) here today. The Minister has worked tirelessly for the first 18 months of our mandate to create real jobs in the country. She has dedicated herself to this cause 24 hours a day, seven days a week. We all recognize the great achievements which have been made-the 580,000 new jobs which have been created. These are real jobs, jobs which involve training and real work experience. In retrospect, when we discuss unemployment insurance, the more people we put into the workforce the less likely it will be to rely on the unemployment insurance system.
Unemployment insurance, or UI, has played an important role in the Canadian economy since its inception in the 1940s and, more specifically, in the last few years. It is a vital social safety net which benefits millions of Canadians every year. In 1985 the UI program paid more than $10 billion to over three million Canadians. This money was paid to Canadians who had lost their jobs and their incomes-Canadians who needed help.
The motion before the House questions changes we have made to the UI regulations. I am glad to see that so many Members are interested and concerned about UI. I think that the interest shown by the House highlights the urgent need to examine the UI program.
The purpose of UI is to help alleviate the effects of unemployment and to help people get back on their feet quickly. We are not sure that the present structure of the program does this. As most Hon. Members are aware, the Government has commissioned a complete review of the UI program. The Commission of Inquiry on Unemployment Insurance, chaired by Claude Forget, who, I might add, is a distinguished Canadian and who had the honour of representing in the provincial legislature the same riding which I represent federally, spent several months travelling across the country listening to the views of all Canadians.
We feel there is an urgent need to overhaul the UI program to make it responsive to the needs of Canadians and to take its place in the economic framework of the country. None of us can deny the beneficial effects of UI, especially during hard times. We must accept the responsibility of maintaining those beneficial effects, if not improving them. At the same we must not lose sight of our managerial responsibility.
In 1985 the UI program cost us over $11 billion. We must contain the costs of the program within reasonable levels to ensure that we can continue to afford it. We must ensure that
the program survives. The basic premise of unemployment insurance is that people who lose their jobs can get money while they are looking for another job. This basic premise is not always easy to define.
The Hon. Member thought that I was wrong in what I said before. It is more than likely that I was not as clear as I might have been since I know I am right. I do not want to say that the Hon. Member is wrong in light of his distinguished service to the House. However, what I did say is that to have access to UI benefits a worker has to demonstrate that he has no earnings coming from his employment and that he has worked long enough to be qualified. For sure he has to be unemployed. This is something that he will have to prove for everey week he will be claiming UI benefits. The starting point is for a worker to be without work and without pay for at least seven days. This is called an interruption of earnings. While on claim these same people must be looking for work. They must be available at all times for work. These are the basic principles of unemployment insurance.
As originally conceived, the design of unemployment insurance was based directly on the principles of a social insurance program. Emphasis was given to limiting benefits to instances of unforeseen and unavoidable risk of unemployment. Coverage was limited to workers in this category and benefits were based directly on the concept of insurable risk. This meant that there was a direct relationship between the extent of attachment to the labour market and the eligibility for and duration of entitlement to benefits.
During the period of some 30 years between 1940 and 1970 there was a decreasing emphasis on strict insurance principles and an increasing stress on other social and economic objectives. In particular, coverage was extended to workers in seasonal occupations where it could not be argued that the risk of unemployment was unforeseeable. In fact, it was quite the opposite-a recurring yearly event.
In 1970 a new program design was introduced to make the program more relevant to the changed socio-economic conditions of the 1970s. This was embodied in the 1971 legislation. In part, this involved the establishment of a new relationship between insurance and non-insurance principles. For example, initial benefits were related to labour force attachment and extended benefits related to local unemployment conditions.
As it turned out a combination of the designed features of the 1971 Act and the changing conditions in the economy and labour market, particularly high unemployment, gave greater weight to the income transfer aspects of the scheme. These circumstances led to a significant extension of the program and its costs, as well as an increased proportion of total cost allocated to the government account.
In 1971 the Liberal Government reduced the eligibility requirement to just eight weeks of work during the previous year and lengthened the maximum duration of entitlement to 44 weeks. As a direct result UI expenditures leaped from $700 million in 1970 to almost $2 billion in 1972. Currently, unemployment insurance is the most expensive operating pro-
March 20, 1986

gram of the federal Government, costing us $11.6 billion last year. To give a comparison, we spent $8.9 billion on defence.
Following 1971, a series of legislative amendments was introduced over several years to contain the expansion of the program, to redress the balance between insurance principles and income transfer considerations, and to ensure a more positive effect on the labour market. Despite these amendments, fundamental concerns remain about the objectives and design of the program in the context of dramatically changing conditions in society, the economy and the labour market. Since 1971 these many changes, both legislative and regulatory, have resulted in a progressively more complex program of patchwork. All the changes were attempts to make the UI program adhere more strictly to its basic principles, but many have had the effect of making the program more and more complex.
When the Government took office in 1984 it inherited the UI program and the responsibility to administer it. On November 8, 1984, the Government announced its intention to make changes to UI, and these changes were in response to its managerial responsibility. It was important that some action be taken quickly to help give order to the patchwork.
The changes were announced in the economic statement of November, and a press release was sent out in December, 1984, to a list of over 7,000. All media outlets were covered. The press release covered the announced changes and the implementation date. In March, 1985, a letter was sent out to 650,000 employers, all employers participating in UI, notifying them of the pension regulation change. It would seem to me that this was more than adequate notice.
UI is an insurance program based upon earnings and attachment to the labour force. All the Government has done is redefine the question of earnings to reflect the reality of the situation and has stuck to the principles of UI. There are those who seem to believe that unemployment insurance should operate like a savings plan or a prepaid pension scheme. However, UI is neither of these; UI is not a retirement fund and it is not automatic. All UI claimants must prove that they are eligible and must continue to prove that eligibility each week they are on claim.
As we can see in the motion before the House, even these basic principles of UI are open for discussion. Every Canadian has an opinion on UI. Many of these opinions are often in conflict. We have heard members of the business community tell us that UI is a disincentive to work and that the benefits are too high. They want UI to be more difficult to obtain and to be paid for less time. On the other hand, others have told us that UI did not pay enough and should be paid longer. Who is right? Seemingly there is no natural consensus.
This is why, on July 6, 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced a commission of inquiry on unemployment insurance. The Forget Commission was charged with a comprehensive examination of the UI program. I should like to
Supply
read from the terms of reference of the commission of inquiry, its main responsibilities:
The Commission of Inquiry on Unemployment Insurance will analyse the role of the unemployment insurance program as a means of improving the operations of labour markets in Canada, to more effectively support Canada's economic development as an equitable financing partnership of business, labour and government, and to provide new and better opportunities for Canadians experiencing temporary unemployment.
It is an all-encompassing review of the UI program. In addition, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has specifically requested that the Forget Commission look at the question of earnings. For this reason, we look forward to receiving the recommendations of the Forget Commission to continue the evolution of unemployment insurance in Canada.
As many of my colleagues are aware, the best solution for UI is to find jobs for people. We have accepted the responsibility of putting the country back to work. When our Government came into office in September, 1984, it became immediately apparent that dramatic changes were needed to the existing complement of federal job-creation and training programs. The programs in existence at that time were inadequate. We soon discovered that most of the job-creation programs were short-term and make-work in nature and did nothing to address the need for meaningful, enduring employment, not only for older workers but indeed for workers from all age groups, while much of the training being provided was irrelevant to the real needs of the Canadian labour market.
Facing record unemployment levels and rapidly escalating demands for skilled and reskilled workers, the Government was not prepared to stand still and watch more and more Canadians suffer from the humiliation of unemployment and underemployment. Accordingly, at the first opportunity during the First Ministers' Conference in Regina in February last year, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Employment and Immigration jointly presented the outline for a bold new initiative which would represent a whole new approach to training and the provision of needed employment for Canadians, termed the Canadian Jobs Strategy. This exciting new approach represents a complete redesign of Government labour market programs and a fundamental change in the way in which we develop and invest in Canada's workforce. It is a change which gives ordinary Canadians suffering from lack of work or from lack of skills the opportunity to get relevant training and relevant experience for the lasting, meaningful employment they must have.
As a Government, we value the opinion of all Canadians. My colleagues have already made reference to the Forget Commission and to the intensive discussions and dialogue with Canadians as part of the thorough review of the UI program. Similarly, in developing the Canadian Jobs Strategy, we consulted with hundreds upon hundreds of individuals and groups across the country. We valued the opinion of the unemployed young person in Cape Breton. We valued the opinion of the older miner who was laid off because of a mine closure in northern Ontario. We valued the opinion of the older woman in Saskatchewan who wanted to re-enter the labour market after many years as a home-maker.

The Canadian Jobs Strategy ensures that federal resources are used effectively to bring direct assistance to those most in need. Many Canadians face severe disadvantages in the labour market or are more severely affected by changing technology and economic conditions. These include the growing number of women re-entering the labour market, the long-term unemployed, workers needing skills training to avoid lay-offs or job displacement, and workers in communities suffering economic decline who need new opportunities for long-term employment. All these groups include older workers to a large extent.
Job training, job creation and economic development are linked to provide these Canadians with valuable skills, practical work experience and meaningful employment opportunities. The re-entry option under the Job Entry Program is helping many older women who have been out of the labour force for at least three years and may require career counselling and instruction in job search techniques or skills upgrading due to new technology in the workplace to re-enter the workforce.
In Kamloops, British Columbia, under the re-entry option 15 workers are receiving class-room training and practical work experience over a period of 34 weeks, to prepare them for work in the automated business office. Of these, six are over 45 years of age.
In metropolitan Vancouver, 50 workers are being trained in management skills for business including computer applications, supervision and management skills, and computer literacy for 31 weeks. Of these 50 workers, 16 are over 45 years of age.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy is also assisting many older workers under the Job Development Program. Frequently, older workers are eligible for the Job Development Program because they have been out of work for 24 weeks of the past 30 weeks. In Quebec, a non-profit agency is giving 42 forestry workers an opportunity to develop specialized skills to improve their ability to adapt to changes in their industry.
Older workers are also finding assistance under the Skill Investmnet Program. This program is the first one to help employed older workers to plan for change in advance. They can train for the future before their existing skills become obsolete. For older workers it is a chance to get the skills they need for continuing employment. For employers it is a practical way to avoid laying off adaptable, capable older employees during times of change.
This is not the only way employers and employees can benefit from skills training under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. The Skill Shortages Program provides much needed financial assistance for employers who must train workers in skills in short supply and high demand.
In Newfoundland, a company seeking to stay competitive in a changing market is modernizing its plant by installing a beam line conveyor system, a system which will help the company increase its productivity and throughput of structural steel. For this piece of technology to operate effectively, it is
necessary for a number of employees to have developed skills as both fitters and welders. The Skill Shortages Program is assisting in this effort by providing training which will eventually permit eight employees to become certified welders. Two of these trainees were chosen from among the senior fitters in the company. They had 26 and 13 years of experience respectively, and despite the fact they were not the younger employees of this company they accepted the challenge with enthusiasm and dedication.
The Community Futures Program will also benefit many older workers in communities across Canada experiencing economic decline, chronic unemployment, plant closures, massive lay-offs or the disappearance of single industries.
These are some of the examples of what we have done for older workers. We have remained consistent with the basic principles of UI while introducing innovative programs to help older Canadians who are looking for work. We must continue to help individual Canadians adapt to a changing world while still providing assistance to those Canadians who need our help.
We are anxiously awaiting the recommendations of the Forget Commission so that Ul can be more effective, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity given to us by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) through his motion, seconded by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). I have listened carefully to the debate which has taken place this morning. 1
March 20, 1986

think it would be worthwhile to read the motion to the House again because there seems to be some confusion in the debate as to what the motion actually asks for. The motion reads:
That this House recognizes the unnecessary hardship inflicted on older Canadian workers by the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which cause pension benefits to be considered earned income for unemployment insurance purposes, and since votes on opposition motions are no longer considered a question of confidence in the Government, therefore urges the Government to repeal those changes immediately.
I think this is a reasonable motion which is obviously well thought out. It is moved in the spirit of what is right and fair with regard to unemployment insurance premiums. It is also moved in the spirit of the new parliamentary reform of which every Member of the House is supportive. It gives Members on the Government side an opportunity to vote, based on the needs of their own constituents, without threatening the Government with defeat. It allows individual Members of Parliament to represent the interests of their own constituents.
As has already been pointed out, I and other Members have received numerous petitions from our constituents. There is a deep concern about what the Government has done to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It behooves all of us to express those concerns in a very clear way. The Government has indicated it does not feel that strongly about the measure. If the Forget Commission recommends that this measure be reversed, then the Government has indicated a willingness to do so. In fact, two Ministers of the Crown have made special pleas to the Minister to not proceed with this change in regulations. So there is a broad base of support for what this motion expresses.
Before I go on to some other remarks I feel I have to comment on two or three of the interventions that were made following the Parliamentary Secretary's remarks. I may be wrong in what I heard, but I understood one Member to ask the Parliamentary Secretary a question concerning massive abuse of unemployment insurance. Apparently there are all kinds of people making fraudulent claims against unemployment insurance. Is the Government looking into that? I have had an opportunity over the years to look into this matter, and if there is an update on the data I would be pleased to hear it. It is my information that of all claims Filed for unemployment insurance less than one-half of 1 per cent are considered to be fraudulent. People apply for unemployment insurance because they need financial support while they are unemployed. They do it honestly and forthrightly. If I am correct in my understanding of what that particular Member asked, that is totally unfair based on the facts as I know and understand them to be.
If you look at the insurance industry as a whole, whether it be car insurance, home insurance, fire insurance or any other kind of insurance, if they had a fraudulent rate nearly as good as one-half of 1 per cent, it would be outstanding. The unemployment insurance fund is well-controlled and well-policed. Sometimes it is policed too harshly. When the UIC throws a wide net to try and identify fraudulent users, very
Supply
often many innocent claimants are caught up and quite unfairly denied benefits.
To get back to the motion itself, the reason the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt and his colleagues in the NDP felt it was important to have this subject debated in the House was specifically because the Government did not make this change in that way. It was done by Order in Council. Members from all sides were not given an opportunity to debate what the Government did at the beginning of this year. We have not had a chance to vote on this measure. The unemployed were never asked whether they thought this was a good or bad idea. They have since expressed their opinion through petitions to Parliament; they do not like it. This is true of not only unemployed workers but also people who are working and who may face unemployment some day. They view it as a bad thing and for a very good reason.
Many of the people who are signing these petitions have worked hard all their life. Many of them have been in the workforce for 30-odd years. They paid unemployment insurance premiums in the expectation that if they ever did become unemployed they would receive some income. They had expectations and those expectations are being denied to them by what this Government is now doing. It is changing the rules in midstream and that is what strikes people as being totally unfair. It is not only inequitable, it is totally unfair.
The Government keeps telling us that it is taking a new approach, there is a process of consultation where there never was before. If that is the case, why were the unemployed not consulted? Why was Parliament not consulted? So far as we know there was absolutely no consultation, unless it was with the business community. It certainly was not with the ordinary Canadian. That is why we have this motion before us. Since that consultation did not take place we want to air the matter now in a very public way. We think there is broad general support for this motion in the country. Conservative Members who do not support the motion are going to hear very loudly and clearly from their constituents.
I recall the debate which took place on the Government's plan to deindex Old Age Security payments. The Government told us that there was broad general support from seniors for this program. After those statements were made I watched with great interest who the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was talking to. He did not talk to senior citizens. Even when senior citizens came to Parliament he did not speak to them about the impact that measure would have on them. Every time I observed the Minister he was in New York talking to U.S. businessmen, in Montreal talking to Canadian businessmen, or in Toronto talking to financiers. He never spoke to senior citizens or future senior citizens about what he was trying to do to their pension income. However, once the seniors caught on to what the Minister was about to do they consulted among themselves and voiced their concerns in a very concerted way. The Minister saw the justness of their arguments and reversed himself. That is all this motion is asking for. It asks the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to come to her senses, do the right thing by the

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a year ago today the arts community marched on Ottawa to protest cut-backs in spending stemming from the Government's first economic statement. As a result of that and other protests across the country, the Government learned to listen. It has even responded by the appointment of numerous task forces to investigate various aspects of the arts, such as broadcasting, film distribution, museum and arts funding.
However, concrete support for the arts community is still inadequate, and the election promises made to it of increases at least to cover increases in the cost of living have not been respected. What the Government calls an increase in the Budget fails to replace the money cut back last year. Further, there has been interference by the Minister in the management of the supposedly independent agencies.
Policies announced by the Government such as those related to the publishing industry are ignored when actual decisions must be made, most notably in the takeover of Prentice-Hall.
It is time for the arts community to come back to the Hill to restate the case that the vital contribution it makes to Canada needs and deserves our full support.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, biotechnology and genetic engineering will, without a doubt, make food production much more efficient in the years to come.
Technological advances will likely change the pattern of agriculture as much in the next 25 years as was the case in the previous 75.
A recent United States study by the Congressional Office of Technology Assessment predicts that only 50 per cent of that country's farmers will still be in business by the turn of the century. Large farms, in proportion, will be able to adapt to a much greater degree than smaller ones.
If we are to stay competitive, and if our remaining farmers are to enjoy a high standard of living, then Canadian longterm agricultural policy has to encourage the adoption of the new techniques and the changes of scale they necessitate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that the Conservatives' belief in the free market system in oil is beginning to unravel, as the free market system is no longer providing the petroleum industry with the high prices the industry had hoped to obtain.
The Premier of Alberta is apparently willing to join with the largest cartel in the world and cut production of oil in Alberta. In this way we can protect both the consumer and the small Canadian producer. In my view cutting oil production does not necessarily help the small Alberta producers.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to focus particular attention on the major agreement on acid rain that was concluded yesterday by the President of the United States and our Prime Minister.
For the first time, the U.S. President has recognized the problem of acid rain and its disastrous effects on our environment. We should welcome this agreement with relief and look forward to an unqualified commitment from the U.S. Congress to release the funds required to reduce acid rain. This agreement between our two governments should have a number of positive repercussions.
I am thinking of a region like Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, where economic activity is very much dependent on our forests, and I am thinking of our pulp and paper industry, and the importance of the sports fishing sector, now that aquatic life is threatened in hundreds of lakes in my region.
We have the Prime Minister to thank for this agreement, and he is certainly the one who brought about this change in attitude within the U.S. Administration. It shows the difference between Conservative co-operation and Liberal confrontation tactics.

speechtext:
In the absence of the Prime Minister I direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerns the subject of the Prime Minister's recent exercise in cosmetic diplomacy in Washington. Apparently the greatest achievement the Prime Minister claims is that he persuaded the President of the United States to recognize that a fact is a fact, namely, that acid rain is an
environmental killer, that it is poisoning North American lakes and rivers, that it is wrecking our drinking water, and that it is destroying our farms. Would the Secretary of State consider this to be anything more than a hollow victory, a victory surrounded by rhetoric, but short and empty of any concrete action?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I regard the accomplishments by the Prime Minister of Canada in the meeting with President Reagan in the last two days to be a very significant step forward on a number of fronts including, most important, the question of action with regard to acid rain. It is most important because the United States administration had the most distance to come.
As the Minister of the Environment said yesterday, it is only a first step. It is a step which was not capable of being accomplished by former Governments of Canada. It has been accomplished by the Prime Minister and this Government. We all looked forward to co-operation across the House, across the continent, and across federal-provincial relations to ensure that we continue to make progress against the enemy of acid rain.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs knows, or he must have read about it, that there is no commitment to any real action, there is no commitment to money unless American industry acts first, there is no timetable, and there is no schedule. Will the Secretary of State acknowledge that what the President of the United States has acknowledged, at the expense of his own environment and of our environment is a five-year delay or a five-year moratorium-no action at all-postponing the problem into the future, while our rivers, lakes, and forests continue to be poisoned?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue to speak to our motion which claims that the Government has been unfair in causing pension benefits to be considered earned income for the purposes of unemployment insurance benefits.
One of the arguments that has not been raised is that pension income is really deferred income. In other words, if an employee did not have a pension as part of a wage package until retirement, that individual would receive higher salary benefits during the period of time he or she is working. Therefore, I suggest that pension income is really deferred income. It is income that an employee would have otherwise received if he or she had not, by agreement or otherwise, delayed the payment of that income until retirement age. It is irrelevant whether or not that employee retires at age 65 or younger. If they had chosen to receive that income during their working life, they would have received it then and the Government would not have any claim today. It seems to me that in all of those cases, what this Government is doing is totally unfair.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, has already pointed out, the total savings to the Government on the backs of unemployed Canadians will be to the tune of some $300 million. That $300 million which comes from the unemployed, who need the money most at that time, is simply just another rip-off when one considers what the Government has already done in the 18 months it has been in office. As pointed out during Question Period and other times-which has never been disputed by the Government-the average Canadian family has received a tax increase of something like $1,300 over the last 18 months since the Government was elected. What the Government is doing here is just simply another grab at the average Canadian taxpayer. Only this time, rather than going after the employed taxpayer, it is going after those who are unemployed. That is totally unfair and unjustified.
A lot of debate this morning dealt with military personnel. There are also other employees in the Canadian economy who are not in the military but who are affected by this policy. In Toronto, for example, the Massey-Ferguson Company has

Supply
decided to close up its operation at its Strachan Avenue plant. Many of its employees are covered by a collective agreement which allows them to retire after 30 years' service. If they had not elected through the collective bargaining process to delay that benefit until such time as they retired, they would have had an increased salary during their working life. Those employees now find that because the company has decided to close up operations they will be laid off, and after all those years of paying into the unemployment insurance fund they will not be able to collect the benefits.
Some Members of the Government have taken issue with Members of the Opposition by saying that the Government did not act hastily, that somewhere or other it had this on its agenda. We are told this is why the Government asked the Forget Commission to look into these matters. If the Government was being fair, forthright and honest with Canadians and with this House, surely to goodness, rather than jump in and do what it did as of the beginning of this year, it could have delayed the process, referred the matter to the Forget Commission-if it felt it was advisable to do so-and wait until the report came down before it changed the regulation. That would have been the fair thing to do with respect to Canada's employees and to this House. At least in that way the Minister could have tabled the document in the House and allowed debate to take place around the document itself.
Rather than do that, the Government changed the regulation by Order in Council without any consultation with the people who would be affected, or their representatives, such as Members of Parliament, and we are forced in order to get the debate into the House to move a motion on an opposition day as was done by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt. I am glad he has done so because he has given focus to this debate to which Canadians can listen. They can watch very carefully how Members of the Government decide to vote.
As I pointed out earlier, under the new system of parliamentary reform this motion will not necessitate the defeat of the Government if Members of the Conservative Party choose to follow their own conscience and the wishes of their constituents by supporting this motion.
I see my good friend sitting opposite, the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis). I can see in his eyes that he is in total sympathy with what I am saying. He comes from a constituency where there are people employed in the automobile industry who are subject to periodic lay-offs. Many of those people believed him and voted for him on the basis of "job, jobs, jobs". Now those employees are finding that the Conservatives did not follow through on the promise of "jobs, jobs, jobs". Instead, what they have is "taxes, taxes, taxes". The average Canadian family will have additional taxes to pay by this change in the regulation, in addition to all the other taxes they have had to endure in the last 18 months.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of general points as they relate to this question in the Province of Newfoundland. The first point is that all Armed Forces personnel in the Province of Newfoundland have been notified that they are not permitted to make representations to the federal Government in terms of disagreeing with this particular measure instituted by the Government of Canada. Members of the Armed Forces in the Province of Newfoundland are not allowed to sign petitions, to write letters or to make representations to Liberal Members of Parliament which in any way oppose this move by the Government of Canada. I do not know of any other example of that kind of action being taken by the Armed Forces in its dealings with its members or personnel in Newfoundland. It is not acceptable for people in the City of St. John's, in Gander or in Labrador to be told they are not allowed to sign a petition, write a letter, make a telephone call or make any representation to members of the opposition Parties. I do not believe this was ever done before by the Canadian Armed Forces. We do not live in a communist state; we have freedom of speech in Canada. For the Armed Forces to dictate like that to its personnel in Newfoundland is absolutely outrageous. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) should intervene. If he caused this particular action to be taken, he should withdraw it; if he did not cause it, he should reprimand the officials or whoever took that action. It is an absolute disgrace that Armed Forces personnel and their families in that province are not allowed to make representations to a politician because the
politician happens to be a member of the Liberal Party or of the New Democratic Party.
Let us look at the effect of this particular measure of the Government of Canada upon Newfoundland. There will be an approximate loss of $65 million, affecting 6,000 Newfoundlanders. Newfoundland has more people per capita who qualify for veterans' benefits than any other Canadian province. That is a somewhat recent phenomenon, because it has been decided that those who were in dangerous waters during the war qualify for civilian war veterans' allowances. We all know the figure which qualifies a person for unemployment insurance as well as the maximum amount and the minimum amount. If we take into account the average amount and the fact that 6,000 Newfoundlanders are affected by this measure, we find out that the amount of money going into the pockets of Newfoundlanders has been decreased by $65 million. That figure is despicable, as are the actual cheques which are being sent out. When a person receives his first cheque for unemployment insurance, it is for the first week of benefits, and two weeks after that he receives his unemployment insurance. He is paid two weeks at a time. As the House knows, unemployment insurance is averaged out to the closest dollar. If we use the divisor of the Government, we discover that in the Province of Newfoundland about 400 people are receiving cheques in the minimum amount, that is, the first cheque for $1 and then cheques for $2 thereafter.

Very briefly, the matter concerns a public servant who has to pay into superannuation versus somebody else in the private sector who pays into an RRSP or other retirement plan. The public servant when he has finished, perhaps taken early retirement, who had worked and paid unemployment insurance, cannot draw unemployment insurance benefits. On the other hand, the man who paid into the scheme can draw unemployment insurance benefits. The absolute unfairness of the system, which the Government of Canada has initiated, is obvious to all Canadians.
Before I conclude I want to say one further thing about Newfoundland. While Newfoundland has large numbers of people on unemployment insurance claims, the Government of Newfoundland is facing a reduction in the amount of money it gets from the federal Government. This is either intentional by the Government of Canada or unintentional because, as you know, Mr. Speaker, our equalization payments in Newfoundland, as they are in Quebec and in a great many provinces, are tied to various economic factors, one of which is the price of oil. If the price of oil goes down $1, the Government of Newfoundland loses about $10 million on its equalization payments.

The Minister is saying "What do you want? Lower oil prices?" If that dollar in the decrease of a barrel of oil were passed on to the consumers of Newfoundland, the slate would be clean. You add up the consumption of oil and gas in the Province of Newfoundland, and you discover that an average $1 increase in the price of a barrel of oil equals about $10 million in increased costs in oil and gas consumption in Newfoundland. You can look at the equalization formula. It is really a form of indirect taxation. Every time the price of a barrel of oil goes up, the consumer pays about $10 million in the Province of Newfoundland, $1 a barrel averaged out. When the price goes up, the Province of Newfoundland then gets $10 million on its equalization payments. It is a form of taxation by the back door. It is indirect taxation. The Minister asks for my preference. I would prefer that the saving in the decrease in the price of oil be passed on to consumers. I would much rather see consumers in Newfoundland with that money than the Government of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, coming back to the EPF situation, I think it is important that Members in this Chamber, when they make a defence or say that they oppose a Government action, at least stay with the facts, and the facts are simply that EPF is going to rise over the next five years. I can give him figures that EPF is projected to go from the last five-year block of $65 billion for those two programs about $90 billion for the next five years.
If Members on the opposite side are fair they will have to recognize that that is not a reduction, that is an increase. I think what they are talking about is that if the present formula had been extended for another five years, the amount of money would have been greater than that which is now included in the legislation. If that is the argument they want to make, that is a fair argument on their part, and I respect that argument, but I do not respect an argument which simply does not square with the facts, because it does not.
Coming back to the motion before us, you will know that the UI program was originally designed in 1940 to promote the economic and social security of workers in Canada by providing them with an income protection from the time they left one job until they found another job. It was that period of time for which unemployment insurance was designed. It was meant to reflect the strict application of social insurance principles and social objectives. Although coverage has been gradually expanded, the adherence to social insurance principles was of prime continuing concern.
By the end of the 1950s 1 think most people would see the program as having been not only expanded, but generally being universally applied under those conditions or those provisions.
The 1960s was a period of greater legislative stability than the previous two decades. There were some changes made to the UI program as well during the 1960s, but they were in response to changes in earnings and living costs. At that time
Supply
already there was a clear indication and a clear sign of the dissatisfaction with the program, and so in the 1970s some fundamental changes to the program were brought in.
In 1971, as I have already indicated, the unemployment insurance program was amended to include two important principles. They are the coverage of all employees who were in insurable employment and also incorporated in this concept was the necessity that workers who suffer an interruption of earnings be eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits.
It is in accordance with these two basic principles that it was determined that earnings arising from employment should be taken into consideration for unemployment insurance benefits. This, of course, was to prevent double-indemnification, which is a founding principle for all insurance schemes. That was the principle in 1971, and Members can go back to that debate and to the Bill to discover it.
The unemployment insurance program, it must be remembered, is not a savings plan, but rather it was to be an insurance plan. I must point out that unemployment insurance coverage should not be dependent upon an individual's likelihood of collecting benefits. I go back to the time when some of us were not in the House in 1971 and the changes that were made. I remember myself being active then in various teachers' organizations. We made the point at the time that we should not be included in the unemployment insurance program as the changes were being made. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) probably remembers that period as well.
We made the point that it was highly unlikely that that group of people would collect unemployment insurance, and the question that obviously followed then was, if we do not collect or are not eligible to collect-because we were not eligible to collect under the agreement with school divisions- why should we then have to pay the unemployment insurance premiums? One of the arguments that was made was that it is a universal plan, you do not know if you will be unemployed at some future point in time, which theoretically is correct. Second, because you were in the labour force you had to contribute to the risk, you had to broaden the base of the risk, and yes, there would be groups and professions in society who would have a lesser likelihood of collecting unemployment insurance, but that did not obviate their obligation to pay into the fund. That was a general insurance principle which was implemented at the time.
What is interesting is to take a look at whether or not that theory, in fact, has been borne out. I do not have the last figures, for example, for the teaching profession, but I do know there was a period of time when a number of people in that profession, as its numbers were being contracted as schools were being reduced because of a reduction in the number of children in school, took new training other than in their profession and were on unemployment insurance and, in fact, collected.

It is important here to note that, yes, there were people at that time who were drawn into the unemployment insurance plan who previously had not been in the old plan, and who said very clearly that it was very unlikely they would collect any benefits from it. I must point out that unemployment insurance coverage should not be dependent upon an individual's likelihood of collecting benefits. That was the principle. Instead, UI is to be viewed as a pooled risk. Thus while the amount of certain individuals' pensions may reduce the amount of benefits to which they are entitled or may even preclude them from receiving UI benefits, they had been protected against the contingency of an interruption in their earnings during the whole time they paid contributions to the unemployment insurance program. It is essentially this protection that their contributions covered. I think that principle we understand, even though sometimes, as I said, it caught people in the net who earlier had not been in the net and might not have wanted to get caught under the changes of 1971.
Nonetheless, it is important to remember that, while collecting unemployment insurance benefits, workers who are unemployed can receive earnings of up to 25 per cent of their weekly benefit rates without those earnings affecting the UI benefits paid in any week of unemployment. As pensions are included under this 25 per cent rule, those with modest pensions will continue to be eligible for UI benefits thus not depriving unemployed workers of much needed basic UI support. Therefore, only those pensioners who receive a substantial pension, exceeding even the maximum amount of unemployment insurance benefits payable, may be precluded from receiving UI benefits when they retire.
I think an equally important issue in this regard is that in addition to providing universal coverage to all Canadian workers the UI program must remain affordable to the taxpayer contributing either through premiums or through taxation itself. That is a principle as well that we should not forget. The Government feels that a claimant with an income from employment should not be treated in the same way as a claimant who has no income when it comes to determining eligibility to unemployment insurance benefits and the amount that should be paid. I do not think we can abrogate our responsibilities for the control of the UI funds by paying benefits to those who do not have an interruption of earnings.
