Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) for placing before the House what is probably the first resolution that can demonstrate that parliamentary reform can work.
I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) illustrated the problem very succinctly this afternoon. We have argued for the entire day, rationally, intelligently and without rancour, a motion to have this House urge the Government to withdraw an offending regulation. Government Mem-
March 20, 1986

bers have heard our case. I am under the impression that all Liberals will support this motion. The New Democrats will vote for it. I suspect that some Government Members will weigh in their minds what the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as the representative of the Government, had to say today and they will weigh what the Liberals and the New Democrats have said. They will weigh in their minds the letter of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), the contents of the letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to that same Minister asking for modification of the offending regulation, and they will weigh what has been said within the Conservative caucus, I assume, by Members of Parliament on the Government side who have been listening to their constituents.
I would point out that the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), a Conservative Member for a long time, has the interests of the Armed Forces at heart. The Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Crofton) also represents an area with a very large military area establishment, and the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) has in his riding a military establishment at Nanoose. They must have been listening to their constituents. I am sure Hon. Members have listened to retired people from the Armed Forces, the RCMP and, indeed, the many other people who have been left out of the protection of unemployment insurance by this offending regulation.
1 know Government Members are evaluating all this. They are under tremendous pressure from their constituents. They know what is fair and what is not fair. And even some of the most prominent members of their own Government have asked that this be changed. This is the essence of parliamentary reform. I do not envy the Government Members. They have two choices. They can support their constituents and fulfil their responsibility for which they were sent to this House, or they can toe the Government line.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare stated that the Government has the right and the responsibility to make decisions and to carry out those decisions. He said: "We have made a decision on this and we will carry it out". I might remind him, however, that the same statement was made in the House week after week with respect to Old Age Security deindexing until the "grey panthers" of this country rose up in such numbers that the Government realized it would be shot into oblivion if it followed through on that ill-conceived decision.
1 would point out to Conservative Members here today that they have a right to vote and they have a responsibility to support their constituents. They must make the judgment with respect to whether or not this move is fair. Indeed, we have made the argument that it is not fair. In fact, there was no consultation. It was simply done in the dark of night in some black cabinet meeting where Ministers decided, without proper guidance and input from their back-benchers with respect to the effect of such a move. Now that the decision has been brought forward in the light of day, constituents have had a
Supply
chance to look at it. People see that they will be adversely affected by it and they say that it is a mistake.
The very softly worded resolution which would change this mistake is before the House today. I would again congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, for identifying this issue which allows an opportunity to Members of the House to vote on it. I think Government Members have not only to weigh the merits of the issue today, they must keep in mind that parliamentary reform is riding on it. It is an extremely unfair move, one which is not only the subject of this Parliament but that of provincial legislatures which will consider the question. The question has been dealt with in the Nova Scotia Legislature. A resolution was put forward from there to the Government of Canada stating that it is wrong and that it should be reconsidered. The British Columbia Legislature will soon have an opportunity to consider a motion such as the one which is before us. Since there are many British Columbians who will be adversely affected by it, I suspect they, too, will judge that it is a mistake. I believe they, too, will send a clear message to Ottawa stating that a mistake has been made. If there is such an unanimous decision reached in the British Columbia Legislature, then I think the Government in Ottawa must re-examine the issue. It would be a mistake for Conservative back-benchers, who must judge the issue and explain it to their constituents, not to support the motion today.
What does the motion ask? It asks that a mistake which has been made be corrected. It is a mistake which withdraws unemployment insuance benefits through the mechanism of declaring severance pay and pensions as income, thereby prohibiting the opportunity to collect unemployment insurance. This is something for which they have paid and which many people before them have had the opportunity to collect. Even today others who find themselves in a slightly different position in relation to the law are still collecting benefits. Examples of that have been put forward to the House. This is a measure which must be changed. The only way it can be changed is for government Members to support the motion. There is no shame in showing such support. I ask Hon. Members at what time they will accept the problem of parliamentary reform. There is no shame in acknowledging that a mistake has been made. The Government's position with respect to Old Age Security illustrates that point. There is no great political difficulty in saying that, perhaps, we should re-examine this particular problem, rectify it and recover the public revenue from other sources more capable of paying. Government Members will have to make this judgment.
The Forget Commission has been referred to many times in an attempt to get out from under the problem. Government Members realize they are in great difficulty with respect to this decision. They seem to say: "Let the Forget Commission report on it". The commission will likely come back with an optimistic view in the fall of 1986. By that time many thousands of Canadians will have lost their unemployment insurance as a result of this mechanism. It can be rectified right

now. It can be rectified with very little dislocation to the Government since most of those who have lost their benefits are still in the appeal process. Indeed, boards of referees across the country are somewhat confused in terms of this matter. Some of them are handing down decisions which deny appeals while others are upholding them. For example, some 20-odd appeals have been upheld in Nanaimo. The process will be carried on to umpires. I imagine that at some point in time the Supreme Court of Canada will be required to make a judgment on it.
This regulation of the Government is unfair. It may even be illegal. It will generate enormous political heat because of its unfairness. Would it not be more simple for the Government to say that it will restore the rights removed and wait for the report of the Forget Commission? Would it not be better for the Government to say that it will develop recommendations from the report for Parliament and let Parliament make the decision as to which way we should go on this issue? That is the correct way to proceed. Again, I emphasize that there is no problem in suggesting that in the application of the regulation we have a problem. That problem can be rectified by withdrawing the regulation, restoring the benefits to the individuals involved and moving on.
I now wish to refer to a number of special cases. The first deals with members of the Armed Forces. In the constituency I represent I have an Armed Forces station at Holberg and there is another at Comox. There are thousands of people who have retired from the Armed Forces who have moved into the area. I estimate we are talking of something in the order of 6,000 people who are extremely upset as a result of the Government's actions. They are upset because of the unfairness of the move. As has been pointed out previously, members of the Armed Forces contribute through premiums to the Unemployment Insurance Program even though they can now never collect. That is unfair. Members of the Armed Forces are put out of the Armed Forces. They do not have a choice with respect to whether or not they are retired. They are put out and that is it. Therefore, because of that particular situation I think it is incumbent upon Parliament to make sure that they are entitled to collect unemployment insurance benefits in order to make the transition. Most members of the Armed Forces who retire do so at a time of life when the transition is extremely difficult and expensive to make. Their children are almost grown and they are usually eating them out of house and home. They are very expensive to clothe. The parents are looking at post-secondary education, whether it be vocational training, university or technical schools. These institutions are not found in close proximity to the areas which I represent. Children of the people in Comox who need to get to postsecondary institutions must travel long distances. They must board out. Their costs are much higher than those of other Canadians. The point I am making is that the House should seriously consider this situation and vote together on it in order to restore those benefits. In this way we can make the adjustment for the people a little more humane. Those people who are told that they must leave their jobs will at least know that
there will be some security provided through unemployment insurance benefits.
Another aspect of the situation is that in planning pension income the unemployment insurance adjustment period is determined in the development of that for an appropriate level of pension. To withdraw it part way through the game is to do an enormous disservice to those people who have contributed and who have served their country. Through no fault of their own they lose their employment and have to go through a very severe financial adjustment. I am certain that all Members of the House feel that a redress should be made for those individuals. It would only be a misguided response to the Government's line which says: "Since you are members of the Government, you cannot vote in favour of this motion". In the spirit of parliamentary reform, members of the Government should be supportive of such a move in the form of the resolution before us today.
There is another issue which involves retired members of the Armed Forces. These people receive small pensions. To try to deal with the latter years of family life, in terms of children leaving home, purchasing new homes and trying to establish themselves in new employment, many of these people must take part-time jobs which pay the minimum wage. They are still required to pay unemployment insurance. When they become ill they cannot collect sick benefits. They cannot collect unemployment insurance when they pick up seasonal work. This is grossly unfair. We should provide individuals at that time of life with some security, and unemployment insurance was a satisfactory mechanism for doing that. It was fair, and it was a mistake to remove it.
The Government has attacked the Armed Forces, the RCMP and the Public Service on another front. When will the Government stop the attack? There was a proposal in the same recommendations of the Conservative Government to deindex the pensions of members of the Armed Forces down to the level of inflation. It is a mistake. Even the previous Government is not without fault here. When inflation rates were running at the 14 per cent level, it felt that an appropriate level of indexation would be down around the 6 per cent and 5 per cent levels. That was absolutely wrong. Those people on small pensions, who earned their qualification when the salaries of the Armed Forces were much lower, were seriously harmed and will probably never catch up on their pensions because of that attack on their pension income. If the Government compounds its mistake of denying unemployment insurance benefits to those members of the Armed Forces who are retiring by deindexing their pensions, a grievous insult would be inflicted on Canadians, and I do not think they will sit down and take it. Indeed, we in the New Democratic Party intend to support them to the fullest, to win back the benefits they have lost and to preserve the ones they have today.
My counterpart in the Comox constituency, Karen Sanford, will be raising this matter in the provincial Legislature of British Columbia. I would be very surprised if both sides of
March 20, 1986

that House did not indicate to the Government of Canada that it made a mistake and request it to make that change. Karen Sanford will be raising that matter on behalf of her constituents, and the Government Members in this House should be raising it on behalf of their constituents as well.
Earlier today a Government Member mentioned that he could not support it because generals would be collecting unemployment insurance. I hope the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) made that comment tongue in cheek. He knows that there are thousands and thousands of non-commissioned officers who are in very serious financial situations because of what the Government has done to date. Because of one or two individuals, the Member would stop this measure from being retracted or removed so that the vast majority of affected people would be allowed to benefit from a program from which the Government intended them to benefit in order to solve their problems. It is a matter of serious concern. We share the concern about certain individuals with extremely high incomes being entitled to this benefit, but we will certainly not harm thousands and thousands of people because of the odd one who slips through. I hope that Hon. Member will in fact vote with us. I know he has many members of the Armed Forces in his area. Also I know that he is concerned about their welfare and recognizes with some apprehension the kind of harm which this measure could cause.
I should like to refer to another area of concern, there are so many. The Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that he had been a teacher in another life; I too was a teacher in another life. I know that it is a demanding profession. After a certain number of years, some teachers feel that they have made a significant contribution and would like to change fields. They opt for early retirement; they take a diminished pension. There is assistance from the unemployment insurance fund to make that transition. The nice thing about it is that someone else comes into the profession behind them. One comes off unemployment insurance while the other goes on it to make the transition into another occupation or another area of contribution. The net effect on the Government of Canada is zero. However, a young person is working and a senior person is retiring or moving into another area after having opted for a much lower pension. It would be deemed fair by most Canadians to say that that is a rational use of public funds-to allow more young people to obtain work and to allow older people who have made their contribution to retire or move into another area in which they would like to make a contribution, possibly at a much lower salary. That use of early retirement is very valid. Teachers are being discouraged from taking early retirement because of the unemployment insurance regulation which cuts the opportunity to make a transition with some dignity and with some financial stability; they are facing the same situation. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that I am 44 years old, l have never been on unemployment insurance and I hope to spend the rest of my life without drawing unemployment insurance benefits. The message we get depends on whom you talk to. We hear people saying when they are 35 or 40, and 1 say they are right: Mr. Hudon or Mr. so and so, I would rather have a job than draw unemployment insurance benefits, because there is nothing more humiliating and distressing for a man or a woman to draw unemployment insurance benefits. And 1 heartily agree.
And now, all of a sudden, Mr. Speaker, one year before retirement, when they do have an income, it is no longer humiliating to draw unemployment insurance benefits, it is almost a right. And who are we talking about now? We are not talking about people in their thirties or forties, but about
the individual who leaves his job, either voluntarily or involuntarily, although in 95 per cent of the cases, at 64 or one year before retirement, it is voluntarily because the companies oblige them to retire early, supposedly in order to create jobs for young people, which are often subsidized by the Government. So we are talking about that kind of person.
They have been telling us from the start: They will lose everything. For a person to lose unemployment insurance benefits altogether, that person has to have earnings of at least $371 a week. March 20, 1986

On December 21, 1984, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) tabled in the House a document announcing changes in the unemployment insurance regulations. I will give you some background information which should be kept in mind.
On November 8 that same year, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) told the House there would be reductions, cut-backs, a new financial course. That is the day he said: "People drawing an income will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits." At least, the income was to be considered as unemployment benefits, as income in terms of unemployment insurance. It was said that we were taking everybody by surprise.
I was then Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration and I even received from Members opposite-I will find those documents-letters stating that we were taking people by surprise. This was on November 8, 1984. We did not stand still between November 8 and December 21, 1984 because we thought perhaps we were taking people by surprise, so we would do something about it. Mr. Speaker, that is why on December 21, before everybody, including the old doctor, we tabled in the House a document stating that income from severance pay would be considered as unemployment insurance income as of April 1, 1985, and income from pension funds would be so considered as of January 1, 1986. That is where we are now! It was announced on December 21.
People have told us that the decision is recent. Naturally, it is recent, but it was announced on December 21, 1984. Members of the Opposition spoke about it at the time and there were articles in the newspapers. In addition, a letter from the Employment and Immigration Commissionners for employers and workers, Mr. Doyle and Mr. Chafe, was sent in March 1985 to 650,000 employers telling them that lump sums received as separation payment must now be considered an income for unemployment insurance purposes. It was also announced even then that, from January 1986, pension from employment would be taken into account for unemployment insurance purposes. This had already been announced, Mr. Speaker.
We are therefore saying that there was no secret. This was public knowledge, there were articles in the national newspapers and even negative comments, but one positive thing was said at the time, namely that the Government was changing one of its rules to make it more equitable and that it wanted to give everyone the right and the time to adjust to this change.
Mr. Speaker, we have been told that this is unequitable. I heard people say this morning that this change is unfair and 1 have also heard some people say: "I have paid the premiums and I am entitled to the benefits." For my part, I do not consider this a good argument.
